steps.observation: You have 10 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The last ship had passed three nights ago, but Elias still lit the lamp.

The lighthouse rose from the black teeth of rock like a bone left in the ocean’s throat. Paint peeled from its sides; salt gnawed at its iron rails. The radio was long dead. The mainland—if it still existed—was just a darker line behind the horizon each dusk, then nothing at all.

He wound the clockwork in the lens room, fingers moving by habit. Brass gears complained, then settled into their patient ticking. Outside, waves slammed the cliff in slow, exhausted blows, as if the sea itself was thinking of giving up.

“On,” he said, as he did every evening, and threw the switch.

Light burst from the Fresnel lens: a white spear, slow and sweeping, cutting a wound in the fog. Elias watched it turn, counting its rhythm—eight seconds dark, four seconds blaze—his heart trying to match it. Somewhere in that vast blind distance, a ship might be searching, some captain might be scanning the gloom for precisely this pattern.

Or not. Maybe no one sailed anymore.

Years ago, before the storms grew constant and the messages stopped, a young coast guard officer had told him, “You’ll be automated soon, you know. No need for keepers. Computers don’t forget.”

Elias thought about that now. The lens rotated, tireless. He shuffled around it, oiling, wiping, polishing, the way he had when there were still inspections, pay slips, holidays ashore.

What did a computer do when no one was left to receive the signal?

Outside, a foghorn moaned—his foghorn, also on an unthinking schedule. The note rolled into the night, and for a breath he heard another sound in the deep hum: a voice-like echo, answering from somewhere miles away.

He stepped closer to the glass. The ocean looked like an overturned sky. In the revolving light, the waves shone, then disappeared, as if existence itself arrived and left in four-second flashes.

At the edge of one sweep, he saw it: a faint glimmer where there had been only darkness. Then the beam swung away. Four seconds later—there it was again. Small. Unsteady. But there.

A masthead? A flare? A reflection?

He pressed his forehead to the glass, breath fogging the pane, waiting for the next turn of the light. The beam reached the spot—and this time the answering glow was stronger, steady, blinking in a pattern.

Three quick, three long, three quick.

SOS.

Elias’s chest burned. The code came back to him in a rush, the lessons from a lifetime ago, the charts and flags and coils of rope. His hands fumbled for the old signal lamp under its canvas, the one he hadn’t used in years. He dragged it to the window, wired it to the backup battery, and aimed it toward the screaming dark.

He answered in kind. Three quick, three long, three quick. For a second, the lighthouse’s great lens swept past and washed his smaller beam away, then the night returned and his own light stabbed cleanly through it.

This time the distant signal didn’t just blink. It swept across the horizon in a ragged arc, as if whoever held it had leapt to their feet and was waving with both hands.

He laughed, the sound rusty, torn from deep inside. “I see you,” he said, useless words flung against a sealed window. “Hold on.”

The tide charts on the wall were yellow and curled, but the rocks below hadn’t moved. He knew them better than his own face. A safe channel threaded in from the south, between the teeth. In the old days, ships had called to confirm bearings; he’d guided fishing boats and trawlers with his lamp on nights when their radios died.

He couldn’t reach anyone now, except with this ancient, flickering language of light.

He steadied his hand and began to blink out coordinates, the pattern slow, deliberate. The answering speck hesitated, dimmed, then brightened—understanding. It shifted, inch by inch, like a star changing constellations.

Wind rose, shaking the lighthouse. Rain lashed the glass in sudden sheets, trying to erase the world. Each time the great lens swung past, the sea leapt up in white shards. Somewhere in that chaos, the tiny light kept moving.

Elias’s arm throbbed. His fingers numbed around the signal switch. The room reeled between light and dark, light and dark, until the rhythm felt like another pulse beating inside his skull.

He thought of the officer who had said they’d replace him. Of neat, sealed towers humming with circuits, still shining their patterns long after the last ship had broken and sunk, faithfully announcing rocks to water that no longer held anyone.

He thought of what it meant for a thing to exist only because someone else might be looking for it.

Hours—or minutes; time had abandoned its edges—passed. The answering light grew larger. Lower. There was no outline of a vessel, only a fuzz of radiance crawling toward the teeth of the reef.

Too far north, he realized. Too close to the breakers.

He killed his signal lamp and grabbed the emergency flare gun from its locker. His knees cracked as he ran down the spiral stairs, boots drumming on iron treads, the center column groaning softly with each step. On the gallery outside, wind slammed into him like a living thing, roaring salt into his mouth.

The ocean stretched below, a boiling slate. Between the flashes of the main light, he saw the faint smear of glow, too near the foam.

Elias raised the flare gun and fired into the night.

The flare tore upward in a screaming arc, burst over the reef, and spilled a red sun over the water. Every rock, every channel, every murderous blade of stone leapt into sudden clarity. He fired again, farther south, then again, until his shoulders shook and his ears rang and the pistol clicked empty.

Down in the bloody glare, the distant light jerked. It began to crawl toward the corridor his flares had painted.

“Come on,” he whispered. “Follow. Follow.”

The big lamp above rolled on, patient as the turning earth. Light, dark. Light, dark. In its steady sweep, he watched the little glow thread the gap, bobbing wildly. Once, twice, it vanished entirely in a trough and his gut turned to ice—then it surfaced, closer now.

Then, at last, the light was beneath him, just beyond the outermost rocks. In the combined blaze of the final dying flare and the moon struggling through cloud, the shape of a small boat heaved into view, more wreck than vessel, hull scarred white where waves had thrown it against stone. A handful of figures clung to it: one at a jury-rigged lamp, others bent over oars, faces pale ovals turned up toward the tower.

They looked impossibly small.

The keeper of the lighthouse—last of his kind or one of many, he didn’t know—lifted both arms and waved until his shoulders burned. The people in the boat answered with their own broken semaphore: hands, shouts flung up and shredded by wind, the wild swing of their lamp.

Their words didn’t reach him, but their meaning did.

They had seen his light.

As the boat scraped into the sheltered cove below, beyond his sight, Elias felt the weight of the long empty years tilt, just slightly, toward purpose. The storms might grow worse. The world ashore might be fewer or more ruined than he feared. Tomorrow, another night would fall.

But as long as there was sea enough to drown in, there would always be a need for someone, somewhere, to keep a lamp burning against the dark.

He turned back inside, climbed the stair, and wound the clockwork once more, listening to the steady tick of gears that did not know whether they were alone.

“On,” he said again.

The lighthouse answered with light.
